p: Thank you, Chair. I have just targeted questions. For the Queens District Attorney, you said you’ve successfully recovered 21 properties related to deed fraud. How many overall cases do you get– or did you get last year? Is it going up in Queens, or are we staying the same?

So, we had many more cases of deed fraud when we first started investigating deed frauds a few years ago. We have about 180 cases right now going on at the same time

with investigations. We’ve gotten, if my memory serves me correctly, about 23 homes back for people over the last year and maybe two years, but it is becoming less because we are very diligent about investigating, and I think people understand that we have a whole, you know, group of folks, Bureau of Housing and Worker Protection, that are investigating these crimes. And not only that, I think it’s important to note, Council Member, that we are getting houses– not only getting houses back for people, but they understand that there’s some accountability for it. But we’re also teaching. We go out into the community. We talk about Acris [sp?]. We talk about nyc.gov where you can register your property so that you know when someone has taken a mortgage out on your property.
No, I appreciate that and just because of time, so–
[interposing] Go ahead.
Did you say how many cases overall you–
[interposing] It’s about 180 cases right now that–
We’re either investigating, have had over the last several years were disposed of.
Okay.
I only know that because someone just asked us.

Yep, no, I appreciate that. It’s a big concern for us in Brooklyn, and similar to our Brooklyn District Attorney, also my community member– I know you all have done a lot of work on this. I know myself, Council Member Ossé and others have been really focused on it. Do you still– I know there was conversation about a specialized Deed Theft Unit– for Brooklyn, sorry. Do you think this is needed to specialize in these cases for District Attorneys where– I mean, specifically for Brooklyn.
Yeah.
But if we have high cases in other places as well.

Yeah. With Brooklyn with the increasing value of homes, especially in central Brooklyn, there’s been, you know, so much attention of people trying to figure out how to take

advantage of homeowners and rip them off, especially a lot of those homeowners are generational families who’ve lived there until we– you know, the true deed owner is an older adult, and we’ve seen a number of scams increasing. I testified, you know, just a little while ago that we would like to have that funded in our office. We have folks who work in the real estate area, but we don’t have a dedicated deed fraud or a housing unit. We have two postings right now asking for lawyers to come to our office and hopefully the City Council can help fund that, because this is really specialized work. We just did a big case this past year. Got a verdict in December where a man was convicted of stealing multiple homes. A number of those homes were returned. But there’s so much more work to be done, and I do–
So, just, yes, you would love that? You would love that unit?
I would love it, and it’s really needed.

I’m trying. I’m trying, but you know, it’s my District Attorney. So, I’m going to be a little respectful. So, the answer is

yes. And then for the Bronx, we just had a really interesting interaction before you all came with the Police Commissioner where two members of the Bronx said– are looking at CrimeStat and saying, like, crime appears to be up in the Bronx, and it was like a 0-100 response that that’s not true, and so, where are we? Like, what– you know, what we give is what we pull from public data. So, is crime up in the Bronx, or– can you set the record straight for us?

No, crime is up in the Bronx. Look, things have been better, but at the end of the day, even though there have been some decreases, we still lead the city in everything. So, you could tell me that crime is going down, but you can’t tell that to Ms. Jackson in Concourse Village, because she don’t see that when she walks to the four train to go to work and afraid that might get shot, you know, as an innocent bystander or whatever the case is. So, the numbers are up because of the disinvestment that is happening in the Bronx. We still have the same neighborhoods that are not getting the services that they need. A lot of these organizations and community-based organizations that

do this work. I appreciate them. I ask the City Council and the Mayor to continue to fund them, but make sure that they're able to have a presence in the Bronx. Some of them don’t. Some of them do. When these new initiatives come about, and I say I need resources, the City will start an initiative in Brooklyn or Manhattan and say well, they have the infrastructure. Well, we need to build the infrastructure–

[interposing] We hear you loud and clear, and I think all of us in the Council want to support that. That's why that quest– the response to that question was so disrespectful, because it’s two Bronx members who live there every day versus some really nice neighborhood in Manhattan. So, you know, I just– I really thank you for clearing that up, and we do agree–
[interposing] It’s a reality.
And know what’s going on in the Bronx.
But you know, the people in the Bronx are still resilient.
Yeah.
And we’re still trying, but we need the help.

Yeah. I have– I’ll come back. You sure? Okay. I just had some questions about discovery and– sorry, not discovery, case processing and discovery. And I don’t know who can answer this. I don’t think everybody needs to answer it. Maybe they– we can just designate one person. But a major driver of the size of the jail population at Rikers is the length of time it takes to resolve many criminal cases, and you know, a central part of that is meeting discovery obligations, it’s the technology to support those efforts. Significant funding has been budgeted for your offices recently related to discovery technology and implementation. The state gave $50 million to your offices for that technology in fiscal year 2024. In FY26 each of your offices was budgeted millions of dollars for discovery implementation. In the Bronx, $15 million for staff, supplies and materials– capital spending in Brooklyn $13.4, Manhattan $11.8, Queens almost $9 million, Staten Island $2.7.

It looks like all of the money has been zeroed out in the Preliminary Budget. Can each of your offices– well, I guess you all need to respond. But can each of your offices please share the status of installing a data management system to store and transfer discovery, and really just like to the point what, you know, what’s left to do?

Well, I know– we appreciate the discovery money, and the history of it is that when those laws were changed, there was no money, right? So, now we’re playing catch-up. Eventually– finally people heard us, right, that we need money or there was unfunded mandates. So, we have that now. But it’s still going to take some time for that to take effect. That’s the problem with it. Technology costs a lot of money and it takes a lot of time to build what is really needed in our offices in order to get that material out. My office has worked diligently, my IT Department as well as working with the vendors that we have hired to get the work done, we’re well on our way now, but it’s going to take a little bit of time in order to see what the results–
[interposing] But your vendors are done? Your systems are set in place, and now you’re just kind of–
Building, building, still in the build stage.
That’s what I mean, like the operation–
[interposing] Yeah, still in the build stage, because at least we have the money to build.
And not the–

[interposing] The thing is that– the thing is that money was a five-year lookout. We’re in year three. So, it’s going to run out and it’s expensive. So we’ll be coming back to you again and to the state in order to make sure we do our mandate. But we’re all doing the best that we can in order to make sure that we comply with that. Because you know, this– these are people’s lives at stake, defenders as well as our victims and the community at large.

Can I just– Council Member Nurse, I’m sorry just to be clear. There was supposed to be like an organically created vendor

that was going to build out for us and the public defenders. That has not been done yet. So, it’s in the process, and some of the money has been spent, but you know, none of the– as far as I know, no, DA’s office has that completely built out yet. It’s all in the process. It’s still ongoing and discovery still continues to delay the process.
And you all have to each pick a different, like procure your own vendor?
I think four of us have the same vendor, and I think Queens has a different vendor.
[inaudible] Nice.
Nice? Yeah.

Yeah, no, so there’s a– yeah, there’s an initiative under the way. The four offices and the Police Department are working with what’s called Nice to build out the case management which will also build out the discovery retrieval collection and turn over to the defense. That continues to work. It’s very complicated because they started from different systems, and they have to integrate with the Police Department system, so it’s underway. In Staten Island we use a

different system, one that is more from the statewide perspective, and so ours already operates. So we don’t exactly have that same problem.
You’re up and operational with your system?
No, we’re not going to use Nice. We use the system–
[interposing] No, but I’m saying– I’m just confirming–

[interposing] Yeah, ours is– ours for the most part operational. We still have problems when we have to download large amounts of information, say people’s cell phones, a lot of body-worn cameras. So, that physical infrastructure problem we have, but in terms of sort of that operating system platform, we have ours in place. But again, we’re much smaller comparatively speaking–
[interposing] No, I understand.
A smaller office, and– but we’ve had one in place.

I think that ours is the closest because the Bronx started first, because

it was all– it was four offices. The Bronx started first. I actually had a meeting with them recently to find out what’s the status. The build is happening. We’re very close to being operational. And I know that the defenders have taken clients of the Nice system as well. So, the Legal Aid Society and I believe Bronx Defenders, also. But you know, there’s always issues and things that we still have to iron out as you build it out. So, we’re the closest. We’ve used the money. We spent about 60 percent of it in order to do the build, but you know, again, like I said, it takes time.

It absolutely takes time. So, we also do not use Nice. So, two years ago we purchased a new case management system which we’re still– we said we purchased, but we are building it out as well. The next year, we had a lot of IT-related expenses including firewalls, servers, storage related to the planned data center. But we are still building it out as well. I have to tell you, I don’t know what we would have done without that funding. Because the new discovery obligations were such that it was so omni– you know, large, that without that funding it would

have been very difficult, but we’re all building out our systems, and it’s getting much better.
I don’t have anything to add to this.

Yeah, no, I guess it’d be good to keep track on that, and I’ll yield the floor, but it just seems like from a systems perspective, if you all are trying to do the same task, I’m unclear why we don’t have a unified system, you know, a Singulair vendor. I'm sure there are a lot of reasons for it that we can follow up with, but it just seems like there might be some cost-savings and efficiency to have a standard system. Thank you, Chair.

Thank you. Thank you so much. Alright, so next hear from Council Member Encarnacion and then Cabán then Gutiérrez, and Sanchez, and then Wong. We’re a little bit behind schedule. We have CCRB waiting, so we’re going to be a little bit tighter with the four-minute rule. Thank you.

Well, I have two DAs in two of my districts. No, but I’ll be quick, because I really just want to– I’ve been here way too

long. So, the Justice Centers, and I hear you Staten Island, I know that the Justice Center is something that you’ve been waiting for. The Bronx does have a Justice Center. It is not a physical location, though. It is not a– like, we’re trying to– and I want to make sure to, you know, address that narrative, because I don’t want it to be looked at as a check box, right? It isn’t a check box. And I– so, from you, DA Clark, is $2 million what you are asking for for the– in capital, for the Bronx Justice Center?

Well, for capital there needs to be an assessment. There’s a lot of issues connected to the capital. So we have a space that’s dedicated. It’s a HRA building. There’s supposed to be a transfer to DCAS. So, you know, that’s an intergovernmental thing that you all have to figure out around, right?
Yes.
And then once whoever the landlord is going to be needs to have the assessment done as to what that capital cost–
[interposing] Capital needs.

Is really going to look like. I could guess and tell you I think it’s going to be about $20 million. I walked through it, right? But what do I know? And by the time it gets done it’s always more money. So, the problem is we need to transfer from one agency to another, and then there needs to be the assessment of what the capital can be, and then move from there. The $2 million is operational.
Operational.

So right now, CJI is– yeah, CJI is in there, right? They’re working doing some of the work, but we need that baseline. So, that $2 million they continue to operate, but the facilities need to be brought up, the outside, the inside–
[interposing] Yeah, I was at the walk-through.

So, that’s what we’re waiting for and that’s what we’re asking that the City do that. That doesn’t necessarily come to me, but I want to advocate for whether it’s DCAS, HRA, or whoever else from the city is going to maintain the building, because it’s a city building– to do that

assessment so that we could start getting those renovations and upgrades done.
Perfect.

And right. So, Staten Island– so Mike and I go through this. Like, we both say neither one of us have one, and we like really don’t because it’s not really– he got capital money. I got operational money, right? He needs operation and a building. I need capital to get it done. So neither one of us really have it until we get the dedicated funds.
Yeah. And the same is kind of the question for Manhattan. I know the Harlem Justice Center exists, but there’s some capital needs for that building as well. Are you aware of any?

I think there are– I think the Chief Judge– I think there’s a number of discussions going on. It was not asked that we had, you know, this year. Certainly we would love to have a physical structure. I think we would, you know, prioritize the ask I made in terms of expanded resources, CJI, but yes, there’s a need.
And the $3 million in state funding that was for the Restore program, is that state funding? Is it–
Yes, that came from the state.
It is, okay, beautiful.

We’re looking forward to putting that to use to get that done. We’re in the process now of interviewing providers to see who is going to be the providers of that. There’s also academic parts of it as well. So, we’re getting close. Final interviews are happening now. We brought down– I think we had 10 vendors that applied. We’ve narrowed it down. We’re doing the final interviews, and then hopefully we’ll be able to get it working.
Okay, perfect. And the asset forfeiture money, the $9 million that you spoke of, is that the full ask? You’re looking for the restoration of the $9 million for the asset forfeiture money?

So, we’ve started, and I would say in the written testimony I broke it out

for the neighborhood navigators which is the BRID program. That’s about $2,500,000 per year to keep it up and running as it is. You know, and the court-based navigators would be about $2 million. That’s the Fortune program.
So, $4 total?
Yeah, $4.5 [sic].
$4 total, okay. That was it. Oh, look, I made it. Alright. Should I just say Council Member Cabán? COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Thank you. As well, I got two DA’s also.

I got you. Oh, okay. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Yeah, you’re across, too. Anyway, I’m standing for no other reason than I have a health condition. I want to start– well, I guess first I want to start with a little bit of a statement. I think it’s obviously really important that we’re strengthening the treatment courts. There’s a lot of room to grow and also make some changes that would strengthen the program. I– there was some testimony about the peer navigator program. I just want to put out there on the record that I

think it’s– I think that is a bit troublesome, because it’s assuming guilt before a person even speaks to an attorney, and that’s the kind of help that I think people should be getting before an arrest and not necessarily funded through a DA’s office. I think if someone is arrested, then we’ve already failed them in servicing them. But that’s just a statement I want to make for the record. It’s not a question. I do want to ask and follow up on the questions that Council Member Nurse asked about some of the discovery. Obviously, you had that state appropriation, the other money that was coming in. I want to acknowledge by the way, Nice, terrible. Like it is– like, I understand that that’s causing you guys a lot of problems and things that are not your fault, and it’s causing the defenders problems. I also think it’s obviously a really big problem when PDFs get sent to defenders that like aren’t labeled. There’s different information that isn’t sorted in any particular way, and of course, that’s causing case delays. So I just want to acknowledge that. But to follow up on the questions that were asked, the money that was allocated, can you confirm just very

quickly, is it all– has it all been– what has been spent so far? And that’s, you know, the– I think the $50 million that was appropriated in FY24 and then FY26 respectively, the Bronx $15, Brooklyn $13.4, Manhattan $11.8, Queens $9, Staten Island $2.7. How much of that has been spent? And then I know DA Clark, you said that you’re the closest to having the system fully up and running. When will each of you– when do you think you’ll have your systems up and running? So, what have you spent? When do you think you’ll be up and running?

I’ll jump in on the funding. So, there’s one allotment, there’s one tranche of money, $50 million for capital funding that came originally and that has– by everyone’s office has been designated for spending. If not actually going through– as you know, Council Member– COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: [interposing] Yes.
To do it, but that’s been implemented. The other was a five-year allotment of $50 million as spread out as you said, and that is programmatic money. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Yeah.

So that’s money that’s spent every year in the budget. So, that’s being spent the first year and second. We’re in the third now. That has been spent and will be spent as part of our yearly budgets. There’s no holding of that money. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: So, you’re not spending– you’re not under budget is what– I guess what I’m asking. You guys are spending at the rate to fill out the five years?
We’re using it to pay our operating costs, our salaries– COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: [interposing] Yeah.

Rent in some cases, things like that. So, that’s part of– and primarily to pay for the expenses of discovery, to hire the extra people who do body-worn camera, to hire the extra ADAs and the list goes on from there. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: The– I want to move into something else, because obviously there’s an interest with all parties to speed up discovery processing, move cases along in the system. Have your offices had direct access– like, would it speed up discovery, I should say, if your offices had direct access to

NYPD databases, including for misconduct? Would things go faster if you had direct access to those databases?

I don’t think so, because we still– we still– first of all, we’re responsible for it whether we have direct access or not. We’re getting it. Even when we get it we still have to sort it out, because– COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: [interposing] Yeah.

Not everything– you know, like anything else, not everything is relevant. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: But you have to wait for them to give it to you, though, right? Like, I mean, you’re waiting for– you’ll say, hey, I want these things. NYPD then has to turn it to you rather than you directly having access and being like, I’ll just take that because I need it. I’ll take that because I need it.

Yes, but I– the same thing for me. I wouldn't want anybody to have open to all my records either. You– there has to be some safeguards there which I appreciate. We’re still responsible for it. We’re trying to get it as best as we can. These discovery tools that we have will

help make it better because we’ll be able to disperse it better. As far as your question is, I’m– like I said, I’m the closest one. We should be up and running by mid-spring. I already had the talk with them. They talked to the defenders. We’re just about ready. We’re ironing out certain things, and I think that– COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: [interposing] Could everybody else just give a quick like when you think you’ll be up and running? And then Chair, I have two more questions and that’s it.
I just– in terms of direct access, I wanted to say one of the big drivers of delay– COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: [interposing] Yeah.

It's not what’s electronic. It’s what’s still on paper. I know that PD has said they’re starting to convert things electronically, but that is still the biggest driver of delays. Trying to track down an individual officer who has written something or has something on paper. But in terms of our ability to move forward, you know, we’re possibly a year or more away from having a system built out by Nice.

COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Okay.
And we’re in the sort of the remediation stage where– you know, where– COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: [interposing] I just want to be mindful of time. I just want a timeline, and–
[interposing] So, we’re far, far. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Okay.
We believe it’s early 2027. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Okay.
The first one, I think– look, in a perfect world, we’re all in the same system. That would be great. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Great, yeah.
I don’t have a firm projection. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Sure.

I think what we haven’t said a lot is that the Nice– I mean, you said– COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: [interposing] But it’s also– but I think it’s also worthwhile and interesting to discuss the fact that like there might

be different perspectives up here even amongst your colleagues. So, that’s–
[interposing] Yeah, no, I’m– but I also think we’ve all been hampered. Certainly, I’ll speak for my office, the Nice discussions and you can see the– COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: [interposing] Yeah.
[inaudible] They have not been seamless, and that’s been– that’s delayed us. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Sure.

And I did want to say on the comment about the peer navigators, our program that we’re advocating for The Bridge is separate and apart. It has no DA. We’re not out– we give them the funding, and they go do it, so I just wanted to say that. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Great, thank you.
Could I answer that one, too? COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Sure.
We’re getting a vendor to handle it. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Okay.

We’re more in line with Queens, I guess, and we’re expecting about 18 months. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Yeah. I think one of my concerns also about the discovery processing and having direct access to the database, at least from a defenders perspective, misconduct. I can’t tell you how many times I litigated a case and it was three, four, five, six, seven months later, whether it was for, you know, pre-trial hearings or the– that we finally find out oh, there’s misconduct, and then we resolve the case the next day. And that’s the kind of stuff that like really we could be making a difference on. That’s a huge deal. The last thing I want to ask is just directed to you, DA Gonzalez. There has been an increase of arrests for what are lower-level offenses like sleeping on the train, and it caused an arrest to arraignment crisis a few weeks ago in Brooklyn to the point where Legal Aid ended up filing a writ about it. Did you push for DOTs– DATs to be issued for those people who were in on bail ineligible offense? Like, what happened there?

So, it was a confluence of a lot of things. B It was the snow storm. bIt was the two holidays. Typically, they have multiple arraignment parts open. You only had one part open, and then there was additionally on top of the all of the storm-related and holiday-related closures, the court house that was closest to the arraignment, that does the arraignments was having some kind of renovation. And so they were using an alternative court house that could– did not have a pen, so they would have to bring one person up at a time. And so it was a confluence of a lot of things. A number of people stepped in to try to remedy, but it was a– COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: [interposing] And I can appreciate that. I guess my follow-up is just were there people there that were processed that were DAT eligible?

I think the answer is yes, and there was definitely conversations around alternative ways to move people from the– you know, from the system. Including, we did a hawk shift, which is, you know– 11 o’clock to–

COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: [interposing] We call it the lobster shift.
Lobster shift, right. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Yeah, they didn’t have them in my time, but I heard they-

So we did– there was a number of efforts. There were a number of efforts to get people out, but it should not have ever happened. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Yeah. I didn’t think I’d ever say lobster shift during a budget hearing. But yeah, I mean, the last thing I’ll say on that is, like if you’re DAT eligible, especially in those circumstances should have DATs, but I appreciate the response. Thank you, Chair.

Thank you. Thank you so much. Next, we’ll hear from Council Member Gutiérrez, then Sanchez, and then Wong, and then we’ll conclude this panel. We have CCRB who has been patiently waiting outside. We’re a little bit behind. Thank you. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: Thank you, Chair. And I have two DAs, but I think I can do it, because

they’re pretty straightforward and your testimonies are very thorough. DA Katz, and forgive me for not knowing this– I just wanted to ask about one of the initiatives in your testimony. I don’t think you named it, but it’s targeted for youth 11 to 18. You said you piloted it in 2021. Can you just share if there are any– what’s the name of the initiative and if there are any partners?

Right. So, I don’t know which ones you’re referring to, but we have several. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: I don’t know either. You didn’t name it. It was launched in 2021, supports youth development. It’s on page three.
Yes. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: And Crime Prevention program.
So, we have several, so I’ll just go through. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: Okay.

So, we have youth initiatives for schools. We have youth initiatives for 11 through 18. We go into the schools. We talk to the students. We have a whole unit that’s about, I don’t know, three or four people– four or five

people, I think, that go into the schools and they talk to the students. We’ve done about 14,000 students so far as we do– COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: [interposing] Okay.

As we go in and we talk not only about gun violence and gang violence. You know, for instance, we had a shooting of a 13-year-old kid– a young man, and the next week we went into the school in the area to talk about gun violence. So, we have a very active group that goes around the borough and does that. We also have internships. We have explorer programs. We try to give– put a face to law enforcement, and we try to make sure that law enforcement is not a foreign entity to our young people. I have to tell you that we have many young people that want to come back year after year which causes some issue. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: For the same programming you mean?
Yeah, it’s programming. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: Oh. Would I be able to touch base with your office afterwards just to check if–
[interposing] Sure. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: The program has touched some of the high schools in my district in my part of Ridgewood?
Which one? COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: Yeah, I’m not actually– I’m really not sure. So I can do that offline, though.
Pierre Lazo [sp?] in my office is here. He’s head of the youth program and he can give you any information. Pierre is– yeah. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: Great okay I’ll walk over there in a minute.
Yep. He can give you any information on a specific schools that we have gone into, but we’ve been requested by a lot of schools to go in and talk. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: Okay. Thank you.

Thank you. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: Thank you so much. And then DA Gonzalez, I wanted to ask– there was a significant amount in your testimony about just the cost of rent and the space. What are the conversations with DCAS like? Is this not a

city-owned building? I’m sorry that I don’t know this, but kind of what– what is the pipeline for getting you all, like, physical space. And I know that DA Katz you mentioned that in your testimony as well. And then my last question, I’m really interested in your– some of your requests, DA Gonzalez, about data storage and IT staff. If you can just let me know if in your testimony, is this additional requests that you’re make– like, on top of your current budget? And if you can share if any of these– for example, the data storage and technology, is that something that you’re thinking can be done in-house, if it is being done in-house, or how you all are thinking about it? But I would love to touch offline some of these requests. I’m happy to lend my support for both boroughs. I know you both mentioned it in your–
Thank you, Council Member. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: Thank you.

So, just in general in terms of the housing, the municipal buildings that used to support our office was sold by the City of

New York, and as part of a revitalization of downtown Brooklyn, we became the anchor tenant into a commercial building to guarantee that the, I guess developer, would build that area, and it became Metro Tech and it became what it is today. You know, DCAS has extended our lease for a period of time, and there are conversations around that about what’s– you know, the– what the cost of rent is in that neighborhood. And I’ll just echo that. One of the issues I think that our ADAs struggle with, it’s really not so much the physical– you know, they’re in a DAs office. I think one of their biggest concerns, especially new ADAs, is doing something wrong, and so we try to set up the supervisory structure so they’ll have– always have enough structure. Within a bureau we might have one bureau chief and two deputies, so there’ll be two there all the time and maybe a senior person, too, and then have other people try to create an atmosphere where they’re welcome to ask questions.
